title: Cloud Migration Planning Guide: Practical Evaluation and Implementation
description: A practical Developer Tools guide to cloud migration planning, covering requirements, evidence-based evaluation, a realistic pilot, rollout, cost, and risk controls.
author: PilotStack Editorial Team

sections.title: Problem and Scope
sections.body: Cloud migration planning should start with workload dependencies and business outcomes, not a target date alone. Inventory applications, data stores, identities, network paths, scheduled jobs, and third-party connections before choosing a migration pattern. Write down the intended outcome, the people affected, the current baseline, and what would count as failure. Separate the problem to solve from preferences for a particular vendor or methodology.

sections.title: Requirements and Evidence
sections.body: For cloud migration planning, check business criticality and recovery objectives; dependency mapping; data volume and transfer windows; identity and network design; compliance and residency; performance baselines; licensing; observability; rollback strategy; and ongoing cloud operating cost. Separate mandatory requirements from preferences. Record the evidence source and date for every important claim, and label it as confirmed in documentation, verified in a trial, unclear, or unavailable. For developer workflows, validate repository and CI integration, access controls, test coverage, API limits, observability, and rollback procedures.

sections.title: Evaluation Method
sections.body: Use the same scenario and scorecard for each candidate. Weight requirements before comparing products, score each item against evidence, and record trade-offs instead of hiding them in one overall rating. Include usability, administration effort, reliability, accessibility where relevant, support coverage, export options, and the cost of required add-ons.

sections.title: Practical Pilot
sections.body: Choose a bounded workload and rehearse discovery, transfer, validation, cutover, monitoring, and rollback. Compare record counts and checksums where appropriate, test user journeys and scheduled jobs, and measure performance and cost under representative load. Agree on pass/fail criteria before the pilot begins. Compare results with the baseline and record limitations; do not infer performance at scale from a demo or a small sample.

sections.title: Rollout and Ownership
sections.body: Name a business owner and an operational owner. Document setup, migration or configuration, permissions, training, support escalation, and a rollback path. Start with a limited scope, resolve blockers, and expand only when the agreed acceptance criteria are met.

sections.title: Cost, Risk, and Exit
sections.body: Estimate the full cost over the expected use period, including subscription or usage fees, minimum seats, add-ons, implementation, migration, training, administration, and maintenance. Avoid treating a successful data copy as proof that the application is ready. Plan for DNS and identity changes, hidden dependencies, downtime windows, access control, and the possibility that rollback becomes harder after new data is written. Confirm contract terms, service limits, export and deletion procedures, and the steps needed to move away from the solution.

sections.title: Decision Checklist
sections.body: Choose the option that meets the mandatory requirements with acceptable operational risk, not simply the one with the longest feature list. Keep a migration runbook with an accountable owner, entry and exit criteria, data validation, communications, and a tested rollback path. Record the selected option, alternatives rejected, unresolved risks, cost assumptions, owner, and review date.
